title: Steering interfacial molecular structures by substrate-molecule charge transfer
authors: Benjamin Achatz, Matthias Zeilerbauer, Marco Thaler, Milan Ončák, Shadi Fatayer, Laerte L. Patera
abstract: Intermixed self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) provide a powerful approach for tuning inorganic-organic interfaces, but their local structure and energetics often remain elusive. Here, an intermixed stripe phase of fullerene $C_{60}$ and Zn(II)-5,10,15,20-tetrakis(4-aminophenyl)porphyrin (Zn-TAPP) on a Ag(111) surface is identified, establishing a direct link between molecular assembly and charge transfer. Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy (STS) and Kelvin probe force spectroscopy (KPFS) have been used to map electronic states and local contact potential differences (LCPD). Compared to close-packed $C_{60}$ islands, the stripe phase exhibits a larger interfacial dipole and increased occupation of previously unoccupied $C_{60}$ states, consistent with enhanced charge transfer from Ag(111) to $C_{60}$. Analysis indicates that larger $C_{60}$ spacing in the stripe geometry reduces Coulomb repulsion, stabilizing the intermixed phase and enhancing charge transfer with respect to close-packed domains. These results provide direct evidence of charged $C_{60}$ molecules in stripe structures and guidelines for engineering intermixed SAMs with tailored interfacial electronic properties.
summary: This paper investigates how the arrangement of molecules in an intermixed self-assembled monolayer (SAM) dictates the electronic properties at the interface. Using $	ext{STS}$ and $	ext{KPFS}$, the authors demonstrate that the stripe phase of $	ext{C}_{60}$ molecules exhibits enhanced charge transfer compared to isolated islands. This work provides guidelines for engineering molecular junctions with tailored electronic characteristics.
main_problem: The study aims to establish a direct link between the molecular assembly structure of intermixed self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) and the resulting interfacial electronic properties, specifically charge transfer.
main_result: The stripe phase of $	ext{C}_{60}$ molecules, constrained by $	ext{Zn-TAPP}$ on $	ext{Ag}(111)$, exhibits enhanced charge transfer compared to close-packed islands, stabilizing the intermixed structure by reducing Coulomb repulsion.
method: The research combines advanced experimental techniques like Scanning Tunnelling Spectroscopy ($	ext{STS}$) and Kelvin Probe Force Spectroscopy ($	ext{KPFS}$) with theoretical calculations (DFT) to map electronic states and local surface dipoles.
model_or_system: The system involves intermixed SAMs of fullerene $	ext{C}_{60}$ and $	ext{Zn-TAPP}$ molecules adsorbed on an $	ext{Ag}(111)$ substrate, forming distinct stripe and island phases.
key_observables: Local Contact Potential Difference ($	ext{LCPD}$), $	ext{C}_{60}$ state occupation, interfacial dipole, and $	ext{C}_{60}$ intermolecular spacing.
important_parameters: Interfacial dipole magnitude, charge transfer amount (up to $0.5$ electrons/molecule), and lattice parameters of the porphyrin layer.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on deconvolution techniques to correct for the spatial averaging inherent in $	ext{KPFS}$ measurements, and DFT calculations use specific functionals and basis sets.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $	ext{STM}$ images showing ordered phases, $	ext{KPFS}$ spectra comparing different molecular arrangements, and deconvolution results comparing measured vs. intrinsic local potentials.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the intermixed phase structure, then using $	ext{KPFS}$ and $	ext{STS}$ to measure local electronic properties, and finally using DFT calculations to model the underlying charge transfer mechanisms in both stripe and island geometries.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed, quantitative link between nanoscale structural organization (stripe vs. island) and fundamental electronic properties (charge transfer), which is crucial for designing functional molecular electronic interfaces.
